questions.question: Define a crank, name its parts, give everyday examples, and explain what it converts and how it will be used in the model crane.
questions.expected_answer: A crank is an arm fixed at right angles to an axle with a handle at the free end of the arm; pushing the handle round turns the axle. Examples include the bicycle pedal and crank arm, the windlass over a well, a pencil sharpener, a fishing reel, a car window winder, a meat mincer and a boat-trailer winch. It converts a circular or back-and-forth push into rotation, and in reverse, as in a car's crankshaft, rotation into back-and-forth movement. In the crane the string is wound on a drum such as a cotton reel on a skewer, with a card or wire handle fixed at right angles; turning the handle winds the string and raises the magnet.

questions.question: Explain, using the positions of pivot, effort and load, why the crank is an adaptation of a second-class lever, and show how its mechanical advantage is calculated with an example.
questions.expected_answer: In a second-class lever the load lies between the pivot and the effort, as in a wheelbarrow. In a crank frozen at an instant the axle is the pivot, the effort is at the handle far from the axle, and the load acts on the string at the drum's surface close to the axle, so the load is between pivot and effort; the crank is a second-class lever bent into a circle so that it keeps turning. Mechanical advantage is the handle radius divided by the drum radius: a 90 millimetre handle on a 15 millimetre drum gives six, so a 60 gram load needs only 10 grams of effort, while the handle travels six times as far as the string. A spring balance on the handle at 30, 60 and 90 millimetres shows the force falling as the handle lengthens.

questions.question: Describe the design choices for the crane's crank winch, including handle length, drum size, fixing, a stop and alignment, and the errors to avoid.
questions.expected_answer: A handle of about 60 to 90 millimetres suits a finger and clears the mast, while a drum of about 12 millimetres radius, a cotton reel, gives an advantage of five to seven and winds 75 millimetres per turn. The handle must be at right angles and firmly fixed, by passing the skewer through two card layers glued both sides or binding a wire handle with thread and glue, with a card tube on the tip as a grip. A peg, ratchet or string loop stops the load unwinding when released. The drum is placed so the string runs straight up the mast without rubbing and is wound in one neat layer. Errors: calling the crank first class, a large drum that makes the load too heavy, a handle parallel to the axle, and no stop on the winch.
